entries.title: Pennsylvania Democrats Pile on Fetterman While Senators Stay Silent
entries.summary: A party swap by Fetterman could put any hope of a Senate Democratic majority in jeopardy — leaving his colleagues in a bind over whether to speak out against him.
entries.content:
Pennsylvania Democrats lashed out at Sen. John Fetterman following his surprise video appearance at the Republican midterm convention on Wednesday night, with Rep. Chris Deluzio saying Republicans can “have him.”

But even as the party struggles with whether to denounce Fetterman for the move, his counterparts in the Senate have, by and large, remained quiet.

Senate Democrats are looking to flip four seats in the upper chamber with just weeks to go until the November midterms — and a party swap by the Pennsylvania Democrat would likely put that effort in jeopardy.

One Democratic operative who works with Democratic lawmakers said that senators are likely concerned that publicly criticizing their colleague could only push him away.

“You can’t go around yelling at your coworkers if you have to turn around and do something with them,” the operative said. “That is literally the work of looking toward a governing majority or minority, depending on how this all shakes out in November.”

Another campaign operative granted anonymity to speak candidly told The Washington Sun that he would advise Democrats to start building a “Fetterman-proof majority.”

“If I was a Senate Democrat, I would do anything to flip five seats instead of four,” the operative said. “I would do anything to make sure we can have a Fetterman-proof majority.”

Fetterman said in a statement to The Sun shortly after his video appearance that he had no plans to switch parties, saying “should the Senate flip in November, I will still be the 51st vote that I ran on.”

But his participation in the GOP convention follows months of speculation that he could be considering a move to the other side. The senator, who was endorsed by progressive Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) during his 2023 run for office, has increasingly voted with Republicans on issues like government funding and the Iran war this year and has more frequently voiced his disdain for the left wing of the party.

“I’m always going to stand with America. I’m always going to reject the extremes and socialism and that anti-American way of life,” Fetterman said in his videoed convention appearance.

His appearance also followed reporting in The Wall Street Journal last week that his frustration with the party has been mounting. Fetterman has become exasperated with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and once wrote “I truly don’t care” when aides informed him that Schumer was organizing a special conference call for Democrats, according to the Journal report.

Schumer urged Fetterman to stay in the Democratic caucus while speaking to reporters in July, praising him as a “very good” member of Congress. His comments came after Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Republicans would “welcome” Fetterman into their conference, adding that he’s had “conversations” with the maverick senator about making the switch.

“The people in our caucus very much like him and respect him, and we’re a big tent party. We can have a lot of different views in that party,” Schumer said.

But even as senators — like Sen. Peter Welch (D-Vermont), who told Politico “it’s a waste of energy to get spun up” about Fetterman — refuse to dump on their colleague, Pennsylvania Democrats have piled criticism on the senator.

Rep. Brendan Boyle, who is reportedly mulling a challenge for Fetterman’s seat in 2028, said in an interview with MSNow on Thursday that he “hopes and prays” Fetterman will stay true to his word and remain a member of the Senate Democratic Caucus, but stands by his comments calling him a “disgrace.”

“Obviously, there are all sorts of concerns about Senator Fetterman. I think that’s probably going to continue,” Boyle said. “He has always been, throughout his career, a guy who will do the performative stuff. The things that will get him the most attention.”

And Rep. Madeleine Dean, another Pennsylvania Democrat, also expressed concern about Fetterman’s convention appearance. At a Democratic counterprogramming event in Dallas, Dean said she was “disappointed” by Fetterman’s “stunt.”

“We can see in his work ethics that he’s just not present. He doesn’t participate much at all in his own committees, let alone attend them,” she said. “From the ground, from suburban Philadelphia, my constituents are livid. Those who went out and knocked doors for him — they are absolutely livid.”

entries.title: Vance Urges Hesitant Voters to Shelve Concerns Over Iran War
entries.summary: The vice president asked Republicans not to “throw out the baby with the bath water” if they disagree with the administration’s foreign policy.
entries.content:
Vice President JD Vance urged voters uneasy with the Iran war to stick with Republicans for the midterms, acknowledging the conflict’s unpopularity among Americans as it stretches past six months.

The vice president’s appeal to Republicans on day two of the party’s midterm convention in Dallas marked a crucial point in the administration’s recognition of how unpopular some of their policies are among members of their base ahead of November.

Vance said he was speaking directly to voters on the fence and people “who love some of our policies but maybe don’t agree with others.” Referencing the late conservative commentator Charlie Kirk, who died a year ago on Sept. 10, the vice president asked voters to coalesce around Republicans, even if they disagree with the White House’s actions.

“Do not throw the baby out with the bathwater. Don’t give the country over to a bunch of crazy people because you happen to disagree with us on a policy issue here or there,” Vance said on Thursday.

“I’m not asking anybody to agree with me on every single policy of the administration,” the vice president added. “What I am asking you to do is to recognize the contrast with the radicals and recognize the achievements of the last 18 months.”

In his 40-minute speech, Vance didn’t express opposition to the war, which is widely unpopular: Roughly two-thirds of Americans — and an even greater percentage of young voters — oppose the conflict, according to a July poll from The Associated Press.

Vance briefly mentioned young men throughout his speech, also while referencing Kirk. Some young men have said they are disillusioned by the president’s second term, with Trump’s approval rating among the group sinking by about 10 percentage points earlier this year.

Trump downplayed those concerns when Fox News’ Laura Ingraham asked about “demoralized” young male supporters during an interview that aired earlier Thursday evening.

“I don’t think they’re demoralized — I think they’re very proud of the fact that I’m not letting Iran have a nuclear weapon,” Trump said. “I disagree with you.”

In between hammering Democrats on affordability and promising additional economic boosts should Republicans maintain congressional control, Vance also spoke at length Thursday about Americans’ “birthright” ownership over the country. He cited an inaccurate figure of 25 million immigrants allowed through the border under the Biden administration and cast undocumented immigrants as responsible for employment and housing shortages. The vice president said Americans had grown tired of factory closures, overdoses and rising costs.

“We were tired of being called racist for noticing that our country was becoming dirtier and poorer and less safe and less prosperous,” he said.

When a protester interrupted waving a flag, Vance derided the person’s prop as anti-American for several minutes, prompting long cheers from the audience.

“Well, my friend, if you love Mexico so much, get your ass over there. I’ll buy you the plane ticket,” he said, firing up the arena’s crowd, which chanted “48! 48!” in a reference to a potential future Vance presidency.

The vice president also spent a portion of his remarks mocking Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed — who recently quipped that second lady Usha Vance would not have met her grandfather-in-law because of her race — and Texas Senate nominee James Talarico.

He jabbed at Talarico’s past comments about gender, including God being “non-binary” — remarks the candidate has since walked back.

“I don’t know about you,” Vance said, ”but I never want to see that guy’s web browser history.”

entries.title: Trump Returns to Affordability Messaging as Voters’ Economic Attitudes Sour
entries.summary: The president also doubled down on his desire to send $5,000 checks to American adults, even as some members of his own party question how the proposal would work.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump on Thursday reiterated his promise to distribute $5,000 checks if Republicans retain control of Congress in November, disregarding growing concerns over the proposal in favor of energizing the base on promises to improve affordability.

Trump’s remarks on the second day of the party’s midterm convention in Dallas were shorter and more toned down than his announcement the day before: The president focused on affordability with promises to make permanent his policies cutting certain taxes and prescription drug pricing.

“That alone should get us a big victory in our midterms that are coming up,” Trump said of his prescription drug policies. “Get out and vote, please.”

Trump and Vice President JD Vance’s choice to highlight the economy Thursday evening — without acknowledging recent fallout from the nation’s mounting trade war with Canada or record-high oil prices from the Iran war — reflects voters’ top issue in the final months before the midterms. A growing share of Americans say the administration’s economic policies have worsened conditions in the country, according to a July Pew Research survey.

Trump unveiled his idea to distribute dividends on Wednesday night, telling the crowd that if Republicans win both the House and Senate, “you win with us and you get $5,000.”

The proposition — one of many promises the president has made throughout his tenure to distribute cash or checks directly to Americans — would probably cost over $1.2 trillion and could balloon the federal debt. Trump has not laid out a detailed proposal for how to pay for the dividends, though he suggested tariffs could help fund them while speaking to Fox News’ Laura Ingraham in an interview that aired Thursday evening.

Key Republicans say they were blindsided by Trump’s pledge, noting that the White House did not consult beforehand with GOP congressional leadership, including Senate Majority Leader John Thune. The president told Ingraham he has spoken to Thune and House Speaker Mike Johnson, despite also telling CBS News on Thursday that he doesn’t need the Hill’s approval to go through with the payments.

“I do speak to them. We can do it,” Trump said on Fox News.

“A lot of people think I don’t even need congressional approval because we have made so much money,” he added, saying the country has financially benefited from fees associated with companies such as TikTok and Intel. “I see that some people are saying, ‘That’s communism.’ It’s not communism — it’s actually good entrepreneurship.”

Thune’s and Johnson’s offices did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Democrats and Republicans have largely rebuked the proposition as costly and potentially illegal.

Sen. Angus King (I-Maine) called the decision “flat out illegal,” citing a federal law that prohibits offering payments in exchange for voting behavior, while Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom of California accused Trump of trying to “buy your vote.”

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, a Republican, said the plan would lead to more debt and inflation.

“What I don’t think you want to do is borrow another $1.5 trillion, and then just try to flood that into the economy, because that will lead to more inflation,” DeSantis said at a press conference in Miami on Thursday. He suggested that instead, the president should “cut people’s tax and return it to the people.”

Some elected officials publicly embraced the idea, including Vance, who said on Wednesday that the plan would help Americans share some of the country’s “incredible wealth” — though he did not mention the checks during his Thursday night convention speech.

Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) said in a social media post that he “will get a bill ready so that we can get the Trump Dividend passed immediately after the November 3rd election.”

A campaign text sent to Texas voters Thursday afternoon contained an abbreviated link with an “attachment” for the $5,000 check it said the president “just authorized.” The URL redirects to the WinRed fundraising page for Eric Flores, a Texas Republican running for a U.S. House seat.

Texas state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat running for governor, said in a statement that she supports the idea to send $5,000 to Texans, but “it can’t be about who’s in power — it has to be about giving the people their power back.” She promised that, if elected, she would deliver “$1,500 Corruption Tax Refund checks” to help working families who faced “the cost of [Gov.] Greg Abbott’s corruption.”
entries.author: Torrie Herrington

entries.title: 25 Years Later, 9/11 Fades From Congressional Memory
entries.summary: Less than 10% of lawmakers who were at the Capitol that day are still in a Congress that has no plans to mark a fateful day of its history.
entries.content:
About 10 hours after a pell-mell evacuation from the Capitol building, more than 100 members of Congress returned to send a message that the republic had withstood the most deadly terrorism attack on U.S. soil.

“We, Republicans and Democrats, House and Senate, stand strongly united behind the president and will work together to ensure that the full resources of the government are brought to bear in these efforts,” said Senate Majority Leader Tom Daschle, a Democrat pledging his loyalty to the Republican president, George W. Bush.
Capitol Hill September 11, 2001 (3040x1990, AR: 1.53)After the remarks concluded at dusk on Sept. 11, 2001, they held hands and sang “God Bless America.”

Twenty-five years later, the anniversary will go largely overlooked at the Capitol. Memorial services will be held at the Pentagon and Ground Zero in New York, as well as in southwestern Pennsylvania where a hijacked plane crashed.

The House and Senate are out of session for an extended summer break. Many Republicans are waking up in Dallas after an unusual party convention ahead of the November midterms, a hyperpartisan event in which speakers compared Democrats to the mortal enemy.

The House held six minutes of speeches and a brief moment of silence on Sept. 3 honoring the anniversary.

“We were a different country then. Our country has changed,” Jane Harman, who retired in 2011 after serving 16 years in the House as a moderate Democrat, told The Washington Sun. “I can’t picture us saying the same things now.”

Harman is leading a small group of former members of Congress to meet on the Capitol steps Friday to shine a light on that 2001 moment.

Veteran Republicans, who were on hand back then and have seen the institution change, also doubt Congress could unify like it did in 2001.

“The only time we come together right now is when we see an existential threat,” Rep. Darrell Issa of California, who was a first-year Republican standing three rows behind congressional leaders in 2001, told The Sun. “There isn't a single threat right now that is causing people to put country first.”
Capitol Hill September 11, 2001 (876x876, AR: 1.00)
Some younger lawmakers suggested that their generation helped defeat the terrorists overseas and left today’s Congress dealing with smaller issues — and unsure of how to respond to such a major attack.

“You know why we can't know? Because we sent people like me overseas to fight them over there, so that we had no more 9/11s,” said Rep. Dan Crenshaw (R-Texas), elected in 2018 after a decade as a Navy SEAL

His deployments resulted in two Bronze Stars, one with a “V” for valor, losing his right eye from an improvised explosive device in Afghanistan.

“People wonder what we got for 20 years of war,” said Crenshaw, who was in high school in South America 25 years ago. “Well, that's what you got. You got no more 9/11s.”

It’s hard to imagine today, but in mid-August 2001, 50% of adults approved of congressional performance, according to monthly polling by Gallup.

A month after the attacks in New York City and at the Pentagon, 84% of adults approved of Congress, just below the 90% approval for Bush.

Americans had rallied around their leaders in Washington.

The Capitol, which was the intended target for the fourth plane, opened for business the morning after Sept. 11, and within three days both chambers approved a war resolution.

A few weeks later, Bush signed the Patriot Act into law. Some debates took months or a few years but eventually Congress passed a law to change the radio spectrum so first responders had their own wavelength to communicate; tightened immigration laws to screen for terrorists; created a Department of Homeland Security that reorganized security agencies; and reshaped intelligence agencies under a single director of national intelligence.

“It was a recognition that we had our Pearl Harbor, pretty quickly,” Issa said.

***

Without prompting, each lawmaker and former member can tell their version of that morning.

“I was sitting in the Veterans Affairs Committee, in the Cannon Building, to introduce [a new local leader] to the committee,” Rep. Steny Hoyer (D-Maryland) recalled.

Fred Upton, a Michigan Republican who retired in early 2023 after 36 years in the House, took his usual early-morning route past the Pentagon to avoid traffic. He drove to a Senate-side press conference meant to boost 911 emergency services.

It got canceled once the real 9/11 started to unfold. He drove home to Virginia.

Connecticut Rep. Rosa DeLauro was in a Democratic leadership meeting when an aide came in and turned on the television. “Then the plane was headed to the second tower. Everyone got up, we canceled the meeting,” she told The Sun.

Eventually U.S. Capitol Police started screaming at lawmakers and aides to evacuate the office buildings, as rumors swirled about the fourth plane and more attacks.
Capitol Hill September 11, 2001 (1243x1243, AR: 1.00)“We just ran. We ran out of the building, ran through the streets. No one knew where the hell we were going,” DeLauro said.

Issa was supposed to be at a House Foreign Affairs Committee hearing. Alone in his office after staff had been evacuated, he grabbed the keys to his chief of staff’s truck, went to the basement garage and drove a few other members over to the U.S. Capitol Police headquarters on the Senate side of the complex.

That became the briefing point for most rank-and-file lawmakers. Top congressional leaders had been evacuated to a secure location far outside Washington. Despite some security warnings against returning to the Capitol, both Democrats and Republicans argued for some demonstration of unity.

“The American people needed to know that the government was still standing,” DeLauro said.

At 7:15 p.m., lawmakers walked up to the center steps of the Capitol’s East Front, Republicans and Democrats, members of the House and Senate, all intermixed.

All 10 bipartisan leaders in the front row are long gone from office. Bernie Sanders, then in his sixth House term, stood near the back of the group, almost 15 years away from his first presidential campaign that made him a national figure.
Capitol Hill September 11, 2001 (1990x1990, AR: 1.00)
Indiana Rep. Mike Pence, barely nine months into his first House term, stood next to another freshman Republican, Arizona Rep. Jeff Flake, long before Donald Trump’s presidency defined their political careers.

All told, less than 10% of the members of the 107th Congress are still serving today. In today’s Congress, of the top 12 elected leaders in the four caucuses, just three — Senate Majority Leader John Thune, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Senate Minority Whip Dick Durbin — were in office on 9/11.

Politics hit the pause button back then.

Tom Davis saw the TV coverage of planes hitting the World Trade Center in New York while he was still home in Fairfax County. As chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee, Davis called his staff and told them to go home.

Party committees and candidates for Congress suspended fundraising and political activities for several weeks or more.

In the news media, there were only a few cable outlets along with the national TV networks. Digital news didn’t really exist. Regional newspapers still flourished.

“The way people received their news was pretty uniform,” Davis said.

Super PACs didn’t exist and very few lawmakers worried about an extreme ideological challenge in a primary.

“We didn’t cater to the extremes,” Davis said. “Their worst instincts weren’t rewarded. They were punished.”

***

That era’s lawmakers made their share of mistakes, helping erode America’s faith in its leaders.

Issa and Harman regret their votes for the Patriot Act, which was used by the Bush administration for gathering information on U.S. citizens that lawmakers would later try to rein in.

“President Bush wanted every authority he could have. The FBI saw it as an opportunity, and America was in no mood to overly debate what it took to make us safe,” Issa said.

The Iraq War won support in Congress through false intelligence about weapons of mass destruction. Lawmakers struggled to respond to reports of torture interrogations in U.S. facilities abroad.

And the federal deficit, which Congress and President Bill Clinton had turned into a surplus in the late 1990s, began to mushroom again, on its way to total more than $40 trillion in debt this year.

“In many respects, we lost our way. We made some huge mistakes,” Harman said.

Congress did manage to come together during the 2008 financial crisis to pass a relief package to prevent another economic depression, but years later most voters derided that effort because no Wall Street executives went to prison.

At the start of the coronavirus pandemic, Congress passed massive relief packages totalling trillions of dollars. Its approval rating soared to 30%, the first time in more than a decade that that many Americans had seen it favorably — a far cry from the 50% approval just before 9/11.

Eventually, pandemic-era lockdowns turned into political culture wars across the nation.

For some lawmakers, the closest moment to 9/11 came on Jan. 6, 2021, when the far-right, Trump-infused attack on the Capitol sought to block the certification of Joe Biden’s 2020 victory over Trump.

Once the Capitol was secured, Congress returned to work. Pence, overseeing the Senate debate as vice president, delivered a rousing speech about lawmakers fulfilling their duties, just hours after some of the rioters had chanted “hang Mike Pence.”
Mike Pence,Mitch McConnell (5397x3598, AR: 1.50)He received a standing ovation from both sides of the Senate.

But the House debate had little of that spirit. A handful of Democrats and Republicans needed to be separated during a near-brawl in the chamber.

To this day, Democrats say it’s hard to work with Republicans who have not condemned Jan. 6, especially those who have cheered on Trump’s efforts to wash it away from the history books.

“We believe there were people who participated in encouraging Jan. 6, that are House members, and who tried on that night to rationalize it,” Hoyer said last week.

“Donald Trump ruins and destroys everything, including bipartisanship,” said Rep. Jason Crow (D-Colorado).

Crow, now in his fourth House term, was a senior in college in September 2001. He requested to be let out of his ROTC duties and into active duty in the Army, deploying to Iraq and Afghanistan.

He is now focused intensely on defeating Republicans in November through his role at the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

“I'm going to try to send a lot of these folks packing and send them home, and bring in the next generation of servant leaders who are willing to have the courage to do the job,” the Bronze Star recipient said.

Issa said he tries to hold out some hope that a really existential threat would galvanize today’s Congress, but he has his doubts.

“Is the job important enough to put country first, or can you afford to be petty? And the answer lately is, yeah, we're pettier than we've ever been,” Issa said.

For now, Harman is just trying to shine a light on how Congress responded 25 years ago. Maybe the former lawmakers will sing “God Bless America” again.

“It didn’t matter if the person next to you was a Republican or a Democrat, because America was under attack,” she said. “I think it’s important to honor the memory.”

Photo illustrations by Kainaz Amaria/The Washington Sun

entries.title: Two Sports Labor Giants Join Fight Against College Sports Bill
entries.summary: Michele Roberts and DeMaurice Smith, former heads of the NBA and NFL players’ unions, are lobbying against the PCSA.
entries.content:
With the Senate back in session next week — and with the college football season in full swing — lobbying around the Protect College Sports Act is picking up again.

If you watched even a moderate amount of football last weekend, you know that Nick Saban, the legendary former coach, appeared in a pro-PCSA commercial funded by a group called Saving College Sports. If you turned on ESPN’s College GameDay at a certain time, you would have heard Saban and Pat McAfee discussing how Congress has to regulate the industry, another endorsement of the bill. This week, Saving College Sports is out with another television spot, this one starring Colorado Coach Deion Sanders, as Politico first reported.

With a tight window before the midterms, those pushing the bill are getting heavy hitters to support it in public. On the other side, though, some of the biggest names in opposition have been operating behind the scenes.

Michele A. Roberts was executive director of the National Basketball Players Association from 2014 to 2022. DeMaurice Smith was executive director of the NFL Players Association from 2009 to 2023. Early in the summer, as the PCSA gained traction in the Senate, Roberts and Smith decided to link arms and fight the bill together.

Working with a small group of lawyers and labor advocates, Roberts and Smith — whose involvement has not been previously reported — have provided extensive materials to the Congressional Black Caucus, which has been a major factor in past negotiations on college sports. Smith, a longtime presence in D.C. (where the NFLPA is headquartered), said he has also been in regular communication with Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut, the Democratic senator most publicly opposed to the bill. And on the other side of recess, they plan to keep contacting politicians in both chambers, particularly focusing on members who could be swayed by what Roberts and Smith described as labor and race issues with the PCSA.

“What I find astounding is that all of this is being done without athletes,” Roberts told The Washington Sun last week. “Beyond it being horrific legislation, it’s even being done without the participation of the labor that’s bringing in all the wealth.”

The PCSA has eight co-sponsors, including four Republicans and four Democrats. Before the August recess began, Senate Majority Leader John Thune agreed to hold a cloture vote on the bill once the chamber returned. President Donald Trump has supported it throughout the summer, though the bill would still have to pass through the Senate and House before making it to his desk. To that end, if the Democrats take control of the House in the midterms, that would likely end this round of College Sports on the Hill.

Roberts and Smith are not one brain, but they both believe, more than anything, that athletes should be directly involved in any negotiations for a college sports bill, sweeping (like the PCSA) or otherwise. Further, they believe college athletes should have employment rights, which eventually could allow them to unionize and collectively bargain with their conferences or schools.

The PCSA states neutrality on employment, which its Democratic co-sponsors consider a significant win. The bill’s lead sponsors are Sens. Maria Cantwell (D-Washington) and Ted Cruz (R-Texas), their parties’ top members of the Senate’s commerce committee. When Cruz introduced his ideal version of college sports legislation in the fall of 2023, it included a provision to bar college athletes from becoming employees. The same was true of the SCORE Act, which was crafted and pushed by House Republicans in 2025, all the way to the edge of a floor vote that never happened.
PCSA (5000x3333, AR: 1.50)But while the PCSA does not explicitly ban employment, many labor leaders, including Roberts and Smith, feel that is a smoke screen. Their argument mostly focuses on the bill’s antitrust protections, which would allow the NCAA and conferences to set rules on compensation, eligibility and the transfer portal without the threat of lawsuits. To the labor leaders, that would stunt any future organizing efforts, seeing that the chance to collectively bargain over those issues — compensation, eligibility, player movement — would be a key way to entice athletes to sign union cards.

“Take it out of sports and put it into another context,” Smith told The Washington Sun. “Let’s make the constitutional amendment say there is nothing under the Constitution which would bar or prevent a state from recognizing Black people as citizens. Are you fucking happy with that? No, no, we actually created the 14th Amendment to identify them as citizens. Ding, ding, ding. So why don’t we just say this the other way?”

This is just another example of how, despite the stated neutrality, the employment question looms over the PCSA. If a bill established employment rights for athletes, that would be a non-starter for most Republicans, according to aides on both sides of the aisle. But that won’t stop Roberts, Smith and other labor advocates from pushing for it — or from using it to sway pro-labor politicians against this specific bill.

After Roberts and Smith first discussed the PCSA, they connected with Patrick Bradford, a New York-based lawyer who has worked in college sports for the last five years or so. Roberts is also an advisor to DYK Media, an advocacy group that educates college athletes on labor issues.

“We were trying to get to any member of the Senate and House who we thought would at least give us a meeting and read our materials,” Bradford told The Washington Sun. “Because in truth, the August bill hasn’t been dissected at all.”

When they were considering their ways into Capitol Hill, Bradford reached out to Rep. Glenn Ivey (D-Maryland), having tried a case with Ivey before he ran for Congress. Ivey is a member of the Congressional Black Caucus, or CBC. From the beginning, Smith, Roberts and Bradford, along with the rest of their team, knew that lobbying the CBC should be one of their routes. They had seen how the CBC influenced the demise of the SCORE Act in the House. They also knew that, once again, it would be hearing from HBCUs that support the PCSA.

In the materials they shared with the CBC this summer, they framed the PCSA as a civil rights issue, noting, among other things, that the bill would turn back the clock by restricting the earning power of Black athletes in football and men’s basketball.

In May, in a big final swing against SCORE, the CBC said in a statement that it could not support legislation that would benefit universities and conferences that “remain silent” on Black voting rights “being systematically dismantled across the South.” In August, the CBC opposed the PCSA in a statement, saying “We will not be complicit in efforts to further exclude the interests of Black people by advancing legislation that will determine the economic future of Black athletes, their families, and their communities without their meaningful participation and engagement.”

On the other hand, the United Negro College Fund, which represents 37 private HBCUs, supports the bill. As smaller colleges keep feeling the strain of spending and constant player movement in the name, image and likeness (NIL) era, any bill that regulates those areas is a logical sell to them. The PCSA also includes a federal grant program that would help HBCUs fund the broadcasting of sporting events.

If the bill does make it through the Senate, the CBC would be a bigger factor during negotiations — and potential voting — in the House. The PCSA could, in theory, pass through the House on a party-line vote. But Republicans have a slim House majority, and the expectation is that members of both parties would offer a lot of input.

That’s why Roberts, Smith and their colleagues aren’t limiting their advocacy to CBC members. They plan to phone-bank politicians with their central view, which is that this bill would be a setback for athlete labor.

“The rights conferred in this legislation are a de facto prohibition against organizing,” Roberts said. “All the rules and regulations and powers stay with the NCAA.”
entries.author: Jesse Dougherty

entries.title: MAGA Inc. Has the Cash to Prevent Republican Losses. But Does It Have the Time?
entries.summary: Battling the president’s unpopularity, Trump’s political operation is finally spending on races and preparing to hit the road weeks ahead of Election Day.
entries.content:
DALLAS — President Donald Trump is trying to defy history and stave off the pounding that the party controlling the White House typically takes in the midterm elections. To accomplish that, he wants voters to act like he’s running and use his MAGA Inc. political operation to make it feel like he actually is.

“Pretend I’m on the ballot,” Trump said Wednesday night in a nearly two-hour speech at his party’s midterm convention. “I’m on the ballot. Just one more time.”

White House advisers have said for much of the year that the 80-year-old president plans to aggressively campaign in the final weeks of the race. With the convention wrapped up in Dallas, he’s on the clock.

“The president is focused obviously on helping mobilize the base and get people out to vote,” Rep. Mike Lawler (R-New York) told The Washington Sun on Thursday, ahead of his convention speech with families whose loved ones were killed by undocumented immigrants.

Lawler is locked in a tight battle that could help determine control of the House. Asked where he wants to see the president go first, he was tight-lipped: “I defer to the White House on what they’re gonna do. He’s already come to my district.”
NY: President Trump Speaks At Rockland Community College (4000x2662, AR: 1.50)The White House announced Thursday that Trump would visit North Carolina next week, his first campaign event after the convention. Few additional specifics have been released about the president’s pledged barnstorming, though he has said he’ll focus on what his team believes are the most competitive 35 races across the country.

Questions about the president’s focus, and whether he actually cares who wins the midterm elections, have caused concern among Republicans.

Candidates and party leaders spent weeks publicly asking Trump to unleash his political operation’s cash on the crucial races. After a Trump-affiliated PAC called No Going Back made $68 million in ad reservations, according to AdImpact, allies hope it’s the first step of a multipronged approach.

“President Trump is the unequivocal leader and unmatched motivator for the Republican party who is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress,” White House spokesperson Olivia Wales told The Sun in a statement.

One Republican official told The Sun that the White House is considering more than 30 rallies and dozens more telerallies. The official, like others in this story, spoke on the condition of anonymity to detail private conversations and plans. Voters should also expect to see more Cabinet members fanning out across the country to help the party make its closing pitch, according to two sources familiar with the planning.

“This week was a big preview,” said one MAGA operative familiar with Trump’s political operation. “And it will be a lot more classic politicking.”

MAGA Inc. did not respond to requests for comment.

In Dallas, Cabinet officials took to the convention stage one by one to slam Democrats and paint a dark picture about what would happen to the country if the party wrested control of the House and Senate from Republicans.

One Cabinet official told The Sun that the Hatch Act prevented them from talking directly about their work at a political event, which limited what they could convey to voters. The official said the White House meticulously examined the planned speeches to avoid violations at the convention, limiting what policies they could tout from their professional life in their personal capacity.

One of the few Cabinet members who didn’t take the stage was Energy Secretary Chris Wright, who still came to Texas. A GOP source familiar with his efforts said Wright met with key stakeholders in the energy sector. And the Energy Department announced — with Wright in attendance — that Dallas’ Southern Methodist University would receive a multimillion-dollar grant.

Vice President JD Vance is scheduled to attend his second MAGA Inc. event next week, this time in Kansas. Some Republicans expect more such deployments ahead of November.
JD Vance,Mike Johnson (6000x4000, AR: 1.50)Additional gimmicks, such as the $5,000 “dividend” Trump floated Wednesday night, are also expected to come from the administration, according to the MAGA operative, as the administration tries to win over Americans who cite high prices and affordability as their top concerns in poll after poll.

Whether Trump will embark on a cross-country campaign blitz that rivals his 2018 midterm campaign travel remains an open question to some, even within his own party.

“His presence will actually help in a lot of places. But the more he can boost his approval numbers, the better it will be for the party,” Marc Short, who served as Trump’s legislative director in 2018, told The Sun. Still, he added, “the promises have been made for nine months that he’s going to barnstorm the country and we just haven’t seen it.”

In 2018, the first-term president embarked on a 44-city blitz ahead of Election Day, holding rallies mostly in states where he maintained high support. His main affiliated super PAC at the time, America First Action PAC, spent around $30 million, according to Open Secrets. 

Despite that effort and cash, the Republican Party still lost the House to Democrats.

This time around, the president’s PAC has amassed a massive and unprecedented amount of money. While the most recent Federal Election Commission filing showed the organization’s cash on hand at $404 million, Trump said last week the PAC had nearly $1 billion.

“They're very aggressive about fundraising and they can be because of the incumbency,” said a Republican source close to the president.

But MAGA Inc. has become a boogeyman of sorts as Republicans have raised concerns publicly and in private that the PAC — and by extension, Trump — may not spend enough money to combat the president’s sinking approval numbers, high prices stemming from the Iran war and the historical tradition of the president’s party taking a midterms beating.
Election 2026 Republicans 26253106169053 (5064x3376, AR: 1.50)“What I know to be true is that the people that are in charge truly don't care about public pressure at all,” said one GOP operative close to Trump’s political operation. ”But they value public perception within our party. And if our party is banging down the door, they will then feel pressured to let the president know.”

The PAC’s contributions have started to flow. Last week, it spent $10 million to support Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in his tight Senate race, a financial disclosure filed Saturday afternoon showed.

“I do think there's a sense of relief now that they're coming out of stealth mode with their plans, the division of labor with other groups and party entities is coming into focus, and campaigns and donors have a clearer picture of what to expect,” said Liam Donovan, a GOP strategist and former National Republican Senatorial Committee aide.

Under a new PAC established Sept. 1, called Not Going Back, the president’s political operation has scheduled nearly $60 million in ads for Senate and House races in New Hampshire, Michigan and Ohio, as first reported by The New York Times.

It’s not without precedent. When the political operation used the Save America PAC as the driver for presidential spending, before switching to MAGA Inc., it seeded money in 2022 to the Georgia PAC to fund state-based operatives, according to a source familiar with the move at the time.

Democrats say the change is to shield Trump’s sinking numbers.

“Trump’s consultants are already failing at their attempted MAGA Inc. rebrand,” C.J. Warnke, spokesperson for the Democratic House Majority PAC, told The Sun. “They know he’s underwater in every single battleground House district, which is why they’re trying to hide the truth from the voters.”
